You're retrofitting the shared single-game-hosting landing page component for Nxeon (Next.js/TypeScript marketing site, staging tree at /opt/nxeon-staging — work ONLY in staging, never /opt/nxeon prod. Never run `npm run build`; verify only with `npx tsc --noEmit`).

Context: today, 4 game-landing template DIRECTIONS were built as internal preview routes (noindex): `preview/game-cinematic` (Rust example), `preview/game-editorial` (Satisfactory example), `preview/game-console` (Palworld example), and `preview/game-combined` (Rust example again) — the LAST one, "Combined", is explicitly documented as "the greatest-hits merge" of the other three and was flagged `recommended` in the preview index (`app/(marketing)/preview/page.tsx`). The owner has approved rolling this out to all live game pages.

Nxeon has roughly 19 existing LIVE individual game-hosting pages (e.g. `/palworld-server-hosting`, `/valheim-server-hosting`, `/ark-server-hosting`, `/rust-server-hosting`, `/cs2-server-hosting`, etc. — check `app/sitemap.ts` for the exact full list of `-server-hosting` routes) which are almost certainly all rendered via ONE shared component with per-game data (find it — search `app/(marketing)/` for how e.g. `palworld-server-hosting/page.tsx` is implemented; it likely imports a shared component like `GameLandingPage` or similar and passes a per-game data object, rather than each page having its own hand-rolled markup).

Your job:
1. Find that shared live component and its data source (likely a `PREVIEW_GAMES`-style or `GAME_LANDING_DATA`-style object keyed by game slug — note the preview templates reference a `PREVIEW_GAMES` object with entries like `.rust`, `.palworld`, `.satisfactory` — check if this preview data object is actually DIFFERENT from the real live data source, or if it's the same one).
2. Read `components/marketing/gamelanding/GameLandingCombined.tsx` (the "Combined" direction) thoroughly — this is the target design.
3. Determine the safest migration path: ideally, you make the LIVE shared component render the Combined design (reusing `GameLandingCombined.tsx` or merging its JSX/logic into the actual live shared component), driven by the EXISTING real per-game live data (not the preview's demo data), so all ~19 live pages upgrade automatically once you change the one shared component. This is higher-leverage than migrating pages one by one — but also higher-risk since it touches everything at once, so be careful: preserve each live page's real metadata/JSON-LD/canonical (these are per-game, already correct, don't regress them), and make sure the Combined component's expected data shape (art slugs, feature lists, plan/pricing display, etc.) actually maps correctly onto the REAL per-game data for all ~19 games, not just the 3 demo games (Rust/Satisfactory/Palworld) the previews used. Some real games may be missing a field the Combined template expects (e.g. a specific testimonial, a specific stat) — handle gracefully (sensible fallback) rather than crashing or rendering blank for games without that field, and report which games had gaps.
4. Verify at least 3-4 different real live game pages still render correctly and with sensible content after your change (read the resulting rendered structure/data flow carefully since you can't run the dev server here — reason through it code-level, and flag anything you're not fully confident about rather than asserting it's fine).
5. Run `npx tsc --noEmit` — this change touches many pages via one shared component, so a type error here is high-blast-radius; make sure it's fully clean.

If after investigation this turns out to be too risky/complex to do safely as one shared-component swap (e.g., the data shapes are too divergent per game, or there's no single shared component and it's actually ~19 separate hand-rolled pages), do NOT force it — instead report exactly what you found and recommend the safer path (e.g., migrate the top 3-5 highest-traffic games first as a pilot, or build an adapter layer). Be honest about risk; this is real indexed traffic across your whole game catalog, a broken shared component is much worse than a few unmigrated pages.

Report back (under 500 words): what you found (shared component or not), what you changed, which games you spot-verified and how confident you are, any data gaps found per-game and how you handled them, and `tsc` status.

Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.

Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.

- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

/** Families whose OsTemplate rows are game servers. Plain module (safe to import
 *  from server components and "use server" action files alike). */
export const GAME_FAMILIES = ["minecraft", "valheim", "rust", "palworld", "cs2", "terraria", "ark", "satisfactory", "projectzomboid", "sdtd", "vrising", "enshrouded", "factorio", "gmod", "conan", "unturned", "theforest", "sonsoftheforest", "bedrock", "schedule1", "dragonwilds", "sunkenland", "abioticfactor", "corekeeper", "icarus"] as const;
export type GameFamily = (typeof GAME_FAMILIES)[number];

/**
 * Canonical display name + glyph per family, ALL 19 — the single source of truth
 * for capitalization (e.g. "Garry's Mod", "7 Days to Die", "ARK: Survival
 * Evolved", never a raw lowercase slug). Plain module, so unlike
 * components/marketing/GameLogo.tsx's GAME_VISUAL (which is "use client" and
 * also carries brand gradient colors) this is safe to import from a SERVER
 * component too.
 *
 * FIXED 2026-08-23: the deploy wizard's game picker (app/dashboard/deploy/page.tsx)
 * and the "manage my servers" list (app/dashboard/games/page.tsx) each kept their
 * OWN copy-pasted map with only 6 of 19 games — every other family silently fell
 * back to its raw slug ("sdtd", "gmod", "theforest"...) with no capitalization at
 * all. Both now import this instead of maintaining their own list.
 */
export const GAME_DISPLAY: Record<GameFamily, { name: string; glyph: string }> = {
  minecraft: { name: "Minecraft", glyph: "⛏️" },
  valheim: { name: "Valheim", glyph: "🪓" },
  rust: { name: "Rust", glyph: "🔧" },
  palworld: { name: "Palworld", glyph: "🐾" },
  cs2: { name: "Counter-Strike 2", glyph: "🎯" },
  terraria: { name: "Terraria", glyph: "🌳" },
  ark: { name: "ARK: Survival Evolved", glyph: "🦖" },
  satisfactory: { name: "Satisfactory", glyph: "🏭" },
  projectzomboid: { name: "Project Zomboid", glyph: "🧟" },
  sdtd: { name: "7 Days to Die", glyph: "🪓" },
  vrising: { name: "V Rising", glyph: "🩸" },
  enshrouded: { name: "Enshrouded", glyph: "🌫️" },
  factorio: { name: "Factorio", glyph: "🏭" },
  gmod: { name: "Garry's Mod", glyph: "🧰" },
  conan: { name: "Conan Exiles", glyph: "🗡️" },
  unturned: { name: "Unturned", glyph: "🏝️" },
  theforest: { name: "The Forest", glyph: "🌲" },
  sonsoftheforest: { name: "Sons of the Forest", glyph: "🪚" },
  bedrock: { name: "Minecraft Bedrock", glyph: "🧱" },
  // ── Wave 3 (SCAFFOLD ONLY 2026-08-31, NOT yet orderable — no GamePlan/OsTemplate
  //    seeded; see the review plan). Steam/SteamCMD dedicated-server survival games. ──
  schedule1: { name: "Schedule I", glyph: "💊" },
  dragonwilds: { name: "RuneScape: Dragonwilds", glyph: "🐉" },
  sunkenland: { name: "Sunkenland", glyph: "🌊" },
  abioticfactor: { name: "Abiotic Factor", glyph: "🧪" },
  corekeeper: { name: "Core Keeper", glyph: "🪨" },
  icarus: { name: "Icarus", glyph: "🚀" },
};

/**
 * Family id → art slug for the real key-art bundled at
 * public/games/art/<slug>_poster.jpg and public/games/art/<slug>_hero.jpg
 * (naming differs from the family id for a few titles). Single source of truth
 * for every consumer (GameCoverCarousel, GameCoverTile, GameHero) — was
 * previously copy-pasted separately in GameCoverCarousel.tsx, which is exactly
 * the kind of drift that caused the GAME_DISPLAY capitalization bug above.
 *
 * `poster` is omitted for minecraft (no poster art was provided — it resolves
 * real cover art via a different fallback chain instead). Every family has a
 * `hero`.
 */
/**
 * Family id → the port a customer's game client actually connects to, plus
 * which transport it is reachable on. This is the single source of truth for
 * `worker/provision-health.ts`'s post-boot game-port verification (added after
 * a Terraria order silently sat on an interactive world-selection prompt with
 * no TTY — the container showed "Up" while nothing ever bound the port, and
 * PROVISION reported success anyway).
 *
 * SOURCED DIRECTLY from each family's `docker run -p ...` mapping in
 * prisma/catalog.ts / prisma/seed-wave1-games.ts / prisma/seed-wave2-games.ts —
 * these are the ONLY ports Docker actually exposes off the container, so they
 * are the only ports reachable from outside it. If a game's setup script ever
 * changes its `-p` mapping, this entry must change with it or the health check
 * will probe a port nothing forwards to.
 *
 * `protocol` is not always the game's own play port: several titles (valheim,
 * palworld, vrising, enshrouded, theforest, sonsoftheforest, bedrock) expose
 * ONLY a UDP port in their image — no TCP port is mapped at all, so there is
 * nothing a TCP connect could ever prove for them. Where an image also exposes
 * a TCP port (often RCON/query, e.g. rust's 28016, ark's 27020, factorio's
 * 27015) THAT port is used instead: a TCP handshake is verifiable with a plain
 * connect, and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up,
 * which is exactly the class of bug this check exists to catch — even though
 * it isn't the port the player's game client uses to join.
 */
export const GAME_PORT: Record<GameFamily, { port: number; protocol: "tcp" | "udp" }> = {

content.text:
## Investigation Findings — Do Not Force The Swap

**Shared component confirmed, but the data models are fundamentally incompatible.**

The live component is `components/marketing/GameLandingPage.tsx`, used by all ~19 `*-server-hosting` pages (e.g. `app/(marketing)/palworld-server-hosting/page.tsx`). It's driven not by a central data object but by **inline literal props passed per page** — `hero{title,highlight,sub,primary,secondary}`, `intro[]`, `plans[]{name,price,meta,blurb,popular}`, `why[]{title,body}`, `steps[]{title,body}`, `guides?`, `faq[]`, `related[]`. There is no `GAME_LANDING_DATA` object to point at — each of the 19 pages authors its own copy directly in its `page.tsx`.

The preview's `PREVIEW_GAMES` object (`components/marketing/gamelanding/data.ts`) is a **completely separate, hand-authored dataset** covering only 3 demo games (Rust/Satisfactory/Palworld), and its own docstring says so explicitly: "Nothing here touches the live GameLandingPage." Its shape is much richer: `artSlug`, `accent`/`glow` hex colors, `worldName`, `region`, `boot[]` (5 literal terminal deploy lines per game), `reasons[]` (icon-tagged, exactly 4), `reviews[]` (named testimonials with quotes + star ratings), `ratingAvg`/`ratingLabel`, `kicker`, `headline`/`highlight`, `deck`.

I read `GameLandingCombined.tsx` (1052 lines) fully. `game.reasons` and `game.reviews` are consumed with unconditional `.map()` calls — there's no optional-empty path; the reviews section unconditionally renders a header using `game.ratingLabel`/`game.ratingAvg` and star ratings. None of these fields exist anywhere in the live per-page props for any of the 19 games.

**What would be needed to migrate for real, and why I stopped:**
- `artSlug`/colors: solvable — `lib/games.ts` already has `GAME_ART_SLUG` and `GAME_FAMILIES` covering all 19 families cleanly, so hero/poster art and family lookups are low-risk.
- `plans[]`: live shape (`name/price/meta/blurb`) would need re-deriving into `{id,tier,ram,price,meta,slots?,blurb,features[]}` — `features[]` and numeric `slots` aren't present in live data and would have to be invented per plan.
- `boot[]`, `kicker`, `headline/highlight`, `deck`: hand-authored marketing copy, currently only written for the 3 demo games. Would require fresh copywriting for 16 more games.
- `reasons[]`: could plausibly be derived/trimmed from the existing `why[]` (6 items → 4, plus an icon-key mapping), moderate effort.
- **`reviews[]`/`ratingAvg`/`ratingLabel`: this is the real blocker.** These are fabricated-but-labeled-illustrative testimonials with invented names, quotes, and star ratings. Extending that pattern to 16 more live, indexed game pages means inventing "customer" reviews and star ratings for products with no such backing — a content/trust decision, not an engineering one, and squarely the kind of thing that needs explicit owner sign-off given Nxeon's brand-honesty posture.
- Two of the 19 `-server-hosting` routes (`fivem-server-hosting`, `vpn-server-hosting`) don't even set a `family` prop — they aren't game-family pages at all, so Combined (which is built around `GameLogo`+`family`) can't apply to them unmodified.

**I made no code changes.** Forcing this now would either crash pages (missing required fields) or ship fabricated reviews/ratings across ~16 live indexed pages in one shot — high blast radius, not reversible-cheaply once customers/search engines see it.

**Recommendation:** treat this as a real content+data project, not a prop-passthrough swap. Pilot Combined on 2-3 top-traffic games (Rust, Palworld — already have full demo data) as new hand-authored pages first; get sign-off on whether reviews/ratings are wanted site-wide or should be dropped from the template for pages without real testimonials; then batch-author the remaining games' copy before touching the shared component that all 19 live pages depend on.
